subject: Chemistry
description: Isotopes, fission, fusion, decay types, common reactor fuels, India's nuclear plants

questions.stem: Atoms of the same element having different mass numbers (different number of neutrons) are called:
questions.explanation: Isotopes — same element (same atomic number Z, same chemical behaviour) but different mass numbers (different neutron counts). H has three: protium ¹H, deuterium ²H, tritium ³H. Common confusables: Isobars — different elements, same mass number (e.g. ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca). Isotones — same neutron count, different elements. Isomers (in chemistry) — same molecular formula, different structure. Mass number A = protons + neutrons.
questions.subject: Chemistry

options.option_text: Splitting of a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei

questions.explanation: Fission — heavy nucleus (e.g. ²³⁵U) absorbs a slow neutron and splits into two roughly equal smaller nuclei (e.g. Ba and Kr) + 2-3 free neutrons + ~200 MeV energy. Discovered 1938 by Otto Hahn, Fritz Strassmann, Lise Meitner. Free neutrons can trigger more fissions → chain reaction → atomic energy / atomic bomb. Fusion is the OPPOSITE — light nuclei combine. Sun's energy comes from p-p fusion of hydrogen → helium, releasing far more energy per kg than fission.

questions.stem: Which type of radiation has the highest penetrating power and the lowest ionising power?
questions.explanation: Penetration: γ > β > α (gamma needs lead/concrete to stop). Ionisation: α > β > γ (heavy alphas pack the most charge but get absorbed quickly). Alpha — He nucleus (2p+2n); stopped by paper. Beta — fast electron; stopped by aluminium foil. Gamma — high-energy photon (electromagnetic); needs lead. Neutrons — uncharged, very penetrating, slowed by hydrogen-rich material (water, paraffin).

questions.stem: The 'half-life' of a radioactive isotope is the time required for:

options.option_text: Half of the original atoms to decay
Half of the energy to be released

questions.explanation: Half-life (t½) — time taken for HALF of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay; constant for a given isotope, independent of temperature, pressure, or quantity. Examples: C-14 (5,730 years — used in archaeological dating up to ~50,000 years); U-238 (4.5 billion years — used to date the Earth); I-131 (8 days — medical thyroid imaging); Tc-99m (6 hours — medical imaging). After n half-lives, fraction remaining = (1/2)ⁿ.

questions.stem: India's first nuclear reactor, commissioned in 1956, was named:
questions.explanation: Apsara — 1 MW research reactor at Trombay, commissioned 4 August 1956 by Homi Bhabha. Asia's first nuclear reactor. Used 80%-enriched uranium fuel supplied by UK. Decommissioned 2009; replaced by Apsara-U (2018) using Low-Enriched Uranium. Subsequent BARC research reactors — Cirus (1960), Zerlina (1961), Purnima (1972), Dhruva (1985, India's largest research reactor — 100 MW). Power reactors followed at Tarapur (1969 — first commercial), Kalpakkam, Kakrapar, Kudankulam.

questions.stem: Heavy water (D₂O), used as a moderator in CANDU-type reactors, has deuterium replacing hydrogen. Deuterium contains:
questions.explanation: Deuterium (²H or D) — isotope of hydrogen with 1 proton + 1 neutron. Discovered 1931 by Harold Urey (Nobel 1934). Heavy water (D₂O) is ~10% denser than ordinary H₂O; freezes at 3.8 °C, boils at 101.4 °C. Used as MODERATOR in PHWR (Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor) — slows neutrons without absorbing many of them, enabling natural uranium (cheaper, no enrichment) to sustain a chain reaction. India's PHWRs at Kakrapar, Kaiga, Narora, Tarapur are CANDU-style.

questions.stem: India's three-stage nuclear programme — drawn up by Homi Bhabha — culminates in stage 3 with:

options.option_text: Pressurised water reactors using imported enriched uranium
Thorium-based reactors using U-233 bred from thorium-232

questions.explanation: Bhabha's three-stage programme: (1) Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR) — natural U-238 fuel, produces Pu-239 + electricity. (2) Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR) — burn the Pu-239 from stage 1 + breed U-233 from thorium blanket. India's PFBR at Kalpakkam (started low-power ops 2024). (3) Thorium reactors using bred U-233 — exploits India's vast Th-232 reserves (~25% of world). Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) being developed at BARC. India holds ~9.6 lakh tonnes of monazite (thorium-rich) along Kerala/TN/Odisha beaches.
